videoDescription:

►  Open source tool AIaC: https://eu1.hubs.ly/H02z-GD0

I'm sure you have all heard of ChatGPT by now. It has become a buzzword within days of its release and professionals in all fields, especially in high skilled areas like lawyers, doctors, engineers are questioning whether such AI can actually replace them and work.

So in this video I want to talk about what ChatGPT is and how it even popped up, talk a bit about the organization behind GPT called "OpenAI", which has already created many other machine learning models besides Chat GPT and also explain technically about all that.
And then we'll dive in and actually put ChatGPT to use for some DevOps related tasks.
I really want to see how it can help in generating configuration code for building DevOps processes or different parts of those processes and how well it knows different DevOps technologies, but not just some shallow examples or boilerplate code that I can get from official documentation, but instead also try more fine-tuning and small optimizations in that configuration code.

We're also going to check out an open source command line tool that is built on top of ChatGPT and was specifically created for engineers to generate infrastructure as code templates and more and finally we'll talk about the impact of ChatGPT, the quality and usefulness of such a tool for engineers and whether it will really replace the engineers and to what extent you should be concerned.

Edureka’s DevOps online training is designed to help you master key tools of Devops lifecycle like Docker, Puppet, Jenkins, Nagios, GIT, Ansible, SaltStack and Chef used by a DevOps Engineer for automating multiple steps in SDLC. During this course, our expert DevOps instructors will help you:

In this video we're going to talk about a relatively new hot topic in DevOps and Cloud space, which is “platform engineering”. There is a lot of discussion going on, where some people are asking whether platform engineering replaces DevOps. Many people say it goes hand in hand and is rather an addition to DevOps, but in reality it's a bit more complicated than that. Platform engineering actually changes a lot of established rules we knew about DevOps, SRE and Cloud engineering, it changes the game and introduces some new rules.

So let's clearly define, what platform engineering exactly is, more interestingly, why was there even a need for this new role and how it evolved and of course how it compares to DevOps and Cloud engineering and does it really replace any of these roles?

HERE'S A FULL LIST OF DEVOPS ENGINEER INTERVIEW QUESTIONS
Q1. Tell me about yourself and why you want to work in this DevOps role?

Q3. Why do you want to work for our organization in this DevOps role?
Q4. Tell me about the hardest day you’ve had as a DevOps Engineer?
Q5. What are your strengths and weaknesses?
Q6. You are giving a presentation to a number of non-technical company managers. They have no technical knowledge and they are struggling to understand your presentation. How would you adapt your presentation, so they all understand?
Q7. Where do you see yourself in the future?
Q8. How do you handle stress and pressure at work?
Q9. What does DevOps mean to you and what is its purpose in our organization?
Q10. Tell me how DevOps differs from Agile / SDLC?
Q11. What is an inode on Linux?

Q13. Tell me how you'd go about optimizing a database?
Q14. What is garbage collection programming?

Q16. Explain how you copy a local file to HDFS?

videoTitle: Which One is Right for You? Cloud Engineer vs DevOps Engineer

Those new to the Programming and DevOps world often find it challenging to start their journey due to the missing basic prerequisites. For example, issues with setting up a basic lab environment using VirtualBox, problems with networking, or trouble with working with the Linux CLI or text editors like vi editor. Sometimes there are issues with applications - like getting a sample application to work, problems with getting the dependencies to install correctly or trouble with getting a web server to communicate with a database server. Or, at other times, it's working with data formats like JSON or YAML.

So we have identified a gap, and we believe that this is due to missing some of the basic prerequisites, such as knowing the basics of Linux, the basics of tools like VirtualBox, or knowing the basics of the most commonly used applications like Java, Python or NodeJS or web servers like Apache, NGINX etc. As a DevOps or Cloud Engineer, it is crucial to have these basics cleared. videoTitle: DevOps Meetup Zurich 2024: Platform Engineering
videoDescription:
This video captures my presentation delivered at the DevOps Meetup in Zürich on January 25, 2024, where I delve into the prevalent challenges faced by traditional DevOps methodologies, characterized by isolated teams and fragmented value streams that impede efficiency. It explores DevOps as a holistic culture, mindset, and suite of technical practices designed to foster continuous value delivery, prioritize products over projects, and focus on customer-centric development. Additionally, I introduce Platform Engineering as a strategic evolution of DevOps aimed at mitigating the technical and operational complexities encountered when scaling DevOps in larger enterprises. Highlighting a collaborative project with LGT and Zühlke, I present the Platform Plane case study, demonstrating how an internal developer platform can streamline and standardize DevOps processes across various teams, thereby reducing cognitive load and enhancing productivity. This presentation goes beyond theoretical discussion, offering a hands-on demonstration of the Platform Plane and its functionalities, including Kubernetes as a service, API gateway, and Service Mesh, among others. It illustrates the vital role of Platform Engineering in enabling product teams to adopt DevOps more efficiently and effectively, leading to an optimized development lifecycle.

videoTitle: The future of DevOps and the complexity of Kubernetes
videoDescription:
DevOps Engineer Cherwin Nooitmeer on the complexity of Kubernetes and the future of DevOps.

“The future of DevOps is going to be boring”

What is DevOps?
There are programmers that write software that need to run on computers, we call them servers. And when a programmer writes software, someone needs to put that software on the computers. So people like you and me can access facebook.com and see pictures of cats. Right?

The process from getting the software from a developer to one of the computers that Facebook has, because you can imagine, they have a lot of them. How you do that, that is where DevOps comes in.

So you write software and you have to put it in production. The gap in between, that's where my focus is. And I try to reduce that gap, so it's instant basically.

Why DevOps?
Companies have started to realize, if you have good DevOps processes you can deliver value to the customer faster. You can just outperform all competitors.

What’s the future of DevOps?
The future of DevOps, I hope, from my perspective, is going to be boring. DevOps will develop and become more mature. We will get better tools and better ways of doing things, like testing and doing infrastructure in a way that is reliable and fast. Hopefully, my job will be as a commodity so I can work on other things and add even more value to customers.

What is Kubernetes?
So what we need to do is to make sure we can run software, that we can update it, roll back things, etcetera. These are similar things that every company needs to do.

So Google came and they basically understood and standardized the way of rolling out software and deploying it to users, making sure everything works fine. They basically extracted their learnings into a product. And that product is Kubernetes. People like I use Kubernetes to build platforms so we can enable companies to deliver value to customers faster.

What I do think about Kubernetes is that when people see it, they see it’s awesome and they all try to use it. I think that's a mistake.

Is the hype real?
There’s a lot of hype around Kubernetes. But Kubernetes also adds a lot of complexity. And I think the complexity gets overshadowed by the hype. People think it’s fine and it just works and you can use it.

But what I do think, this complexity that is there is necessary. Because if you are not going to use the complexity of Kubernetes, you are going to create your own system that you need to maintain and develop. Because it's not only software that we use to service users. You also need to write software to service the servers, if that makes any sense. Right?

And if you are going to write it yourself. What happens if you hire a new guy? Now you have to explain to the new guy how your complexity works. So instead of using a complexity that everyone knows, you’re going to create your own complexity. And now you have to teach everybody about your own complexity. And then you need to maintain it.

So this is a trade-off, what are you going to do? I mean, if you have a very simple problem and can get away with having less complexity. Then maybe Kubernetes is not the right thing for you.

It’s not about hoping changes work. It’s about knowing you can flip a switch, roll things back, and stay in control when production gets unpredictable.
channelDescription:
LaunchDarkly is the runtime control layer for the AI era. For over a decade we have helped engineering teams control what ships in production, from feature flags to full release governance. Today that mission extends to the AI agents and code that are increasingly building, modifying, and operating software on behalf of engineering teams.

With CodeControl and AgentControl, teams can ship faster, govern what runs in production, and automatically respond when something needs to change, without waiting on a redeploy. LaunchDarkly runs on infrastructure that handles over 50 trillion flag evaluations a day, which means the same platform that governs your features also governs your agents.

Founded in 2014 by Edith Harbaugh and John Kodumal, LaunchDarkly has been named on the Forbes Cloud 100 list and serves some of the most demanding engineering teams in the world.

videoDescription:
I used to be on call 24/7 as a team lead, no vacations, no unplugging. All because of one big lie: that software could be perfect before it hits production.

Reality? It never is.

What actually matters isn’t perfect code. It’s having control. The ability to roll back instantly, fix fast, and adapt when things go wrong.

That’s the shift: from chasing perfection to building confidence in change.
channelDescription:
LaunchDarkly is the runtime control layer for the AI era. For over a decade we have helped engineering teams control what ships in production, from feature flags to full release governance. Today that mission extends to the AI agents and code that are increasingly building, modifying, and operating software on behalf of engineering teams.

With CodeControl and AgentControl, teams can ship faster, govern what runs in production, and automatically respond when something needs to change, without waiting on a redeploy. LaunchDarkly runs on infrastructure that handles over 50 trillion flag evaluations a day, which means the same platform that governs your features also governs your agents.

Founded in 2014 by Edith Harbaugh and John Kodumal, LaunchDarkly has been named on the Forbes Cloud 100 list and serves some of the most demanding engineering teams in the world.

videoTitle: 😱Hey DevOps, you’re killing my job 😢!
videoDescription:
😱Hey DevOps, you’re killing my job 😢!
Really? No 😉.
Don't panic and check out the talk 🎞 I had with Pia Wiedermayer on this topic.

Is DevOps really the reason why testing and quality assurance (QA) employees are being increasingly automated out of a job?
Pia Wiedermayer, Head of QA, and Romano Roth, Head of DevOps, discuss different ways to incorporate the wealth of experience of testing and QA specialists into the agile team culture.

Insight: 
- DevOps is often equated with automation
- What does this mean for people in these roles and with these responsibilities?
- Testers offer a wealth of experience that can be incorporated into the
agile team culture

Software testing and quality assurance are changing. Topics such as agility, DevOps and automation strongly influence existing roles and areas of responsibility in software quality assurance as well as during the entire software life cycle. Standard testing and QA roles no longer exist in many (project) organisations. Dedicated testing teams are increasingly a thing of the past.

What does this mean for people in these roles and with these responsibilities? Is there no room for them anymore? Are their skills and expertise no longer needed?

DevOps is often equated with automation. Is DevOps responsible for automating employees out of a job? What is behind the hype and who or what is DevOps actually?

Pia Wiedermayer, Head of Quality Assurance https://www.linkedin.com/in/piawiedermayer/, and Romano Roth, Head of DevOps, at Zühlke Switzerland tackle these questions. They talk about the challenges in their projects, examine roles and tasks and reveal new paths for professional and personal development. They also discuss ways to incorporate the wealth of experience of testers into the agile team culture and whether automation is the new testing.

The program is designed to provide a holistic understanding of the DevOps principles, tools, and best practices.

Participants in the program gain hands-on experience through practical exercises, case studies, and real-world projects. They learn to leverage popular DevOps tools and technologies such as Git, Jenkins, Docker, Kubernetes, Ansible, and Prometheus. The program also emphasizes the cultural aspects of DevOps, focusing on collaboration, communication, and fostering a culture of continuous improvement.

Upon completing the program, participants have the opportunity to earn a DevOps Certified Professional certification, which validates their proficiency and expertise in DevOps principles and practices. This certification can enhance career prospects and demonstrate a commitment to professional development in the field of DevOps.

The DevOps Certified Professional Program is suitable for professionals from various backgrounds, including software development, system administration, operations, quality assurance, and project management. It is particularly beneficial for individuals seeking to transition into DevOps roles or enhance their existing DevOps skills.

Overall, the DevOps Certified Professional Program provides a comprehensive and structured learning path for individuals looking to build a strong foundation in DevOps practices and technologies. videoTitle: They claim that "DevOps is dead". You won't believe what happens next!
videoDescription:
"DevOps is dead!" Either this is just clickbait from companies that want to sell you their products or services in Platform Engineering or they do not understand what DevOps is.

𝐃𝐞𝐯𝐎𝐩𝐬 is a 𝐦𝐢𝐧𝐝𝐬𝐞𝐭, a 𝐜𝐮𝐥𝐭𝐮𝐫𝐞, and a set of 𝐭𝐞𝐜𝐡𝐧𝐢𝐜𝐚𝐥 𝐩𝐫𝐚𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐜𝐞𝐬. It provides communication, integration, automation, and close cooperation among all the people needed to plan, develop, test, deploy, release, and maintain a product and deliver continuous value to the customer.

𝐏𝐥𝐚𝐭𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐦 𝐞𝐧𝐠𝐢𝐧𝐞𝐞𝐫𝐢𝐧𝐠 is the discipline of designing and building toolchains and workflows that enable self-service capabilities for product teams that deliver continuous value to the customer.

𝐒𝐢𝐭𝐞 𝐫𝐞𝐥𝐢𝐚𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐢𝐭𝐲 𝐞𝐧𝐠𝐢𝐧𝐞𝐞𝐫𝐢𝐧𝐠 (𝐒𝐑𝐄) is a discipline of designing , developing, and maintaining highly reliable software systems. 

👉 Platform engineering uses DevOps practices, enabling product teams to do DevOps.
👉 SRE uses DevOps practices to build and maintain highly reliable and scalable systems.

videoTitle: ♾️🛠️CI/CD Pipeline Explained in Tamil🔁 | #thillaithetechie
videoDescription:
✅ Continuous Integration (CI):
✅ CI is a development practice where code changes are automatically built, tested, and integrated into a shared repository multiple times a day.
✅ It ensures early detection of integration errors and promotes collaboration among developers by providing rapid feedback on code changes.

✅ Continuous Delivery (CD):
✅ CD extends CI by automating the deployment process, enabling teams to release software changes to production or staging environments quickly and reliably.
✅ It streamlines the deployment pipeline, reduces manual intervention, and enhances the consistency and repeatability of software releases.

✅ Pipeline Automation:
✅ CI/CD pipelines automate various stages of the software delivery process, including code compilation, testing, artifact creation, and deployment.
✅ Automated pipelines ensure consistency, efficiency, and reliability, allowing teams to focus on delivering value-added features and improvements.

✅ Feedback Loop:
✅ CI/CD pipelines incorporate feedback loops at each stage, enabling teams to identify and address issues promptly, iterate on solutions, and continuously improve software quality and performance.

✅ DevOps Culture:
✅ CI/CD practices are integral to the DevOps culture, fostering collaboration between development and operations teams, breaking down silos, and promoting a culture of continuous improvement and innovation.

videoTitle: Database Performance Monitoring and Tuning with Amazon DevOps Guru for RDS- AWS Database in 15
videoDescription:
Amazon DevOps Guru for RDS is a machine learning (ML)-powered capability that is designed to empower database administrators, developers, and DevOps engineers to quickly detect, diagnose, and remediate a wide variety of database-related performance issues in Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL, Amazon Aurora MySQL, and Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL. When DevOps Guru detects a database-related performance issue (such as resource over-utilization or misbehavior of certain SQL queries), the service immediately notifies you and provides diagnostic information and recommendations to help you resolve the issue quickly. The service can also help you detect potential database issues with your databases early, so that you can prevent them from impacting your users. With DevOps Guru, you can monitor your databases for performance bottlenecks and operational issues—no manual setup, ML expertise, or deep database expertise required. In this session, you will learn the types of issues DevOps Guru for RDS can detect and how to get started today.

Learning Objectives: 
* Objective 1: Learn about the RDS performance monitoring tools that are available.
* Objective 2: Understand concepts in Amazon DevOps Guru for RDS to help you generate insights about your applications.
* Objective 3: See a demo of Proactive and Reactive Insights you can get with Amazon DevOps Guru for RDS.

videoTitle: BTAIH E03 · Mohamed Daoudi, DevOps Engineer · Can AI Replace DevOps Engineers?
videoDescription:
My third guest on BTAIH is Mohamed Daoudi, a DevOps engineer whose path took him from ENSA and self-taught Linux and Docker to early-stage companies, large-scale cloud systems at Oracle, and independent consulting.

We get into what happens when AI stops being a chatbot and starts touching real infrastructure: writing scripts, handling repetitive migrations, executing commands, configuring CI/CD, connecting hosting and domains, and helping ship a working website in less than 24 hours.

It is a practical conversation, not a hype one. Where AI genuinely makes a DevOps engineer faster, where it turns 100 lines into 10,000, and why giving an agent access to your systems is only useful when you still understand the infrastructure underneath it.

About Mohamed

Mohamed Daoudi is a DevOps engineer with experience across startups, service companies, Oracle Cloud and independent consulting. His work has included CI/CD, Kubernetes, cloud infrastructure, incident management and keeping production systems stable at scale.

Find Mohamed

LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/iduoad/
X: https://x.com/MIduoad

About the show

Beyond The AI Hype (BTAIH) is a podcast about AI, engineering, and building a tech career, hosted by Abderrahman Jaize. We talk in Darija, English, and French, usually all three in the same sentence.

Chapters

كيف يؤثر الذكاء الاصطناعي على حياتنا اليومية؟ تعرف على المهارات التقنية الأساسية التي تحتاجها للبقاء في سوق العمل خلال العصر الرقمي القادم.

يقدم هذا المقطع نظرة شاملة حول الكيفية التي يعيد بها الذكاء الاصطناعي صياغة واقعنا المعاصر. إذا كنت ترغب في فهم التغيرات الجذرية التي تنتظرنا، فإننا نستعرض هنا كيف أصبحت الأنظمة البرمجية هي المحرك الأساسي للاقتصاد والمجتمع في هذا العصر الرقمي.

سيتعلم المشاهدون أهمية امتلاك المهارات التقنية اللازمة لمواكبة التطورات المستمرة. نناقش بالتفصيل لماذا لم يعد الإلمام بالتقنية خياراً، بل ضرورة حتمية للنجاح المهني والشخصي، حيث يمتد تأثير الذكاء الاصطناعي ليطال كل تفاصيل حياتنا، مما يجعل فهم الأنظمة البرمجية مهارة لا غنى عنها.

اشترك في القناة للحصول على تحليلات أسبوعية حول مستقبل التكنولوجيا، وأخبرنا في التعليقات: ما هو المجال الذي تعتقد أن الذكاء الاصطناعي سيغيره بشكل أكبر في السنوات القادمة؟

videoTitle: Steps to Enable Parallel Jobs In Azure DevOps (AZ-400)
videoDescription:
All you will get information in this Video: https://youtu.be/DBQLl360Mz0

Purpose of Parallel Jobs: The video explains how to enable parallel jobs in Azure DevOps, which is necessary for running CI/CD pipelines.

Creating a Project: Start by creating a project within your Azure DevOps organization, noting your organization URL.

Access Billing Settings: Navigate to the organization settings, select "Billing," and locate the option for parallel jobs.

Parallel Jobs Availability: Initially, new organizations have zero parallel jobs available, preventing pipeline execution until jobs are enabled.

Requesting Parallel Jobs: Users must request parallel jobs through a specific URL provided by Microsoft, as they no longer provide them by default due to past misuse.

Misuse Prevention: Microsoft stopped offering free parallel jobs by default because users exploited them for unauthorized activities like Bitcoin mining.

Request Process: Fill out the form with your name, the same email ID used for Azure DevOps, and your organization URL. Request only private parallel jobs unless you have a valid reason for public jobs.

Approval Timeframe: It typically takes 24 to 48 hours for Microsoft to approve parallel job requests.

Verification: After approval, you can verify the availability of parallel jobs in the Azure DevOps portal under the "Parallel Jobs" section in the billing settings.

Billing Setup for Additional Jobs: For additional parallel jobs, users need an active Azure subscription (e.g., Pay-As-You-Go), and setup billing, linking it to the Azure subscription. This will allow for purchasing more parallel jobs if needed.

videoTitle: DevOps とは？～エンジニアじゃなくてもわかる ITトレンド解説 ～
videoDescription:
DevOps とは？
～エンジニアじゃなくてもわかる ITトレンド解説 ～

★フルバージョンはこちらから無料で視聴できます！
https://majisemi.com/e/c/dynatrace-20210305

はい、マジセミ寺田です！皆さんこんにちは！今日は DevOps について解説をしていきます。
エンジニアじゃなくてもわかるように簡単に解説していきますのでよろしくお願いします！
私はマジセミという、IT関連のWebセミナーを年600回程度運営しています。
他のテーマの動画もたくさんUPしてますので是非そちらもご覧ください！
今日のテーマは DevOps ですね、DevOps ってなに？って思われるかもしれないんですけども"Dev"と"Ops"をくっつけた造語なんです。
"Dev"っていうのは"デブロップメント"システムの開発です。"Ops"は"オペレーション"、システムの運用です。
昔は開発と運用が分かれていて、組織も分かれていて、場合によっては会社も分かれてるケースもよくありました。
なんで分かれていたか？というと性格が違うからなんです。
開発はどんどん良いものを作っていきたいと考えているのですが、新しい機能を動かす時や何らかのイベントがある時はトラブルが起きやすいんですね。
逆にいうと何にも変更がないまま運用している分にはそんなにトラブルは起きません。
なので新しい機能を入れるとか改善するとかそういう事をやりたくないというのが運用チームの立場でなんです。
こういった、今までの組織の在り方を理解した上で、現代ではDX（デジタルトランスフォーメーション）が非常に注目されていますが、その中で重要なのはスピードです。
今まではシステムを開発して機能の改善をして、それが使えるようになるのは１年後だとか短くても３ヶ月後という感覚でした。
しかしその感覚だと追いつかなくなってしまいます。
来週、もっと早ければ明日にでも使って欲しい、とスピードが求められています。
そんな中、今までのように開発のチームと運用のチームが分かれていると、全然スピードが追いつかないという事で、もうその工程を１つにしてしまって、開発したらすぐに運用出来るようにする、といった具合に、そもそもの組織のあり方を含めて根本的に作業の進め方を変えていくというのが" DevOps "の考え方や方法論です。
また、今回のセミナー（https://majisemi.com/e/c/dynatrace-20210305）では2021年の米国の最新動向についても紹介しています。
これは" DevOps "だけじゃなくて他にも"AIOps"や”コンテナ”などの最新動向についても解説していますので、" DevOps "や米国のIT最新動向に関心のある方は見ていただければと思います！

videoTitle: DKT98: IPv8, Terraform 1.15, Terragrunt 1.0, NGINX 1.30 - новости DevOps
videoDescription:
IPv8 уже в драфте, Terraform хоронят в блогах, а одна компания жжёт $7M в год на Claude Code. Собрали новости DevOps, которые вы накидали через бота.

О ЧЁМ ВЫПУСК
Новостной выпуск: накопилось 63 новости, разобрали самое горячее. И снова с нами Ярослав. В этом выпуске:
• IPv8: драфт в IETF - ASN в первых 32 битах, старый IPv4 во вторых. Без NAT и dual-stack, плюс токен-идентичность на каждый девайс
• Terraform 1.15: переменные в source и version модулей, отдельная аутентификация для S3 backend
• "Terraform is dead": разбираем хайповую статью - спека как desired state, Pulumi, CDK и причём тут AI
• Terragrunt 1.0: units, stacks и фильтр по affected-ресурсам через git worktree
• NGINX 1.30: sticky sessions, keep-alive и HTTP/2 к апстримам, Early Hints (103), Encrypted Client Hello
• Экономика AI: Semi-Analysis масштабировала Claude Code до $7M/год, дефицит RAM
• Google Agent Sandbox: новый Kubernetes CRD между StatefulSet и Deployment

Сквозная мысль выпуска: AI ускоряет всё, но без понимания, как работают системы, спека и вайб-кодинг рано или поздно стреляют в ногу.

ГОСТЬ
Ярослав Бледковский - Un-principal SRE, Wargaming

videoTitle: D365 F&O: Setup an Azure DevOps CI Build Pipeline | Part 7
videoDescription:
Set up a CI pipeline for D365 in Azure DevOps. Learn to deploy a Build VM and automate your code builds for team development.

───────────

───────────

0:00 → Intro: Why We Need a CI Pipeline (Continuous Integration)

5:43 → Enabling Continuous Integration Triggers & Path Filters
6:23 → Part 5: Branching Strategy (Rename 'dev' to 'Main')
6:52 → Connecting Visual Studio to Source Control (Team Explorer)
7:19 → Mapping a Local Workspace
7:55 → Adding the Local Project to Source Control
8:34 → Adding the axmodulesbuild File & Checking In
9:12 → Part 6: Creating a New 'dev' Branch from 'Main'
10:06 → Part 7: How the CI Build Process Works
10:23 → Reviewing the Build Stages (Build, Sync, Package)
10:59 → Under the Hood: Pipeline Tasks vs. VM Scripts
11:53 → Part 8: Reviewing the Final Build Artifact
12:27 → Recap

──────────────
💡 What You'll Learn
──────────────

✓ Create a self-hosted Agent Pool in Azure DevOps for D365 builds.
✓ How to deploy a Build VM from LCS and connect it to your pipeline.
✓ Configure an auto-generated build pipeline with CI triggers and path filters.
✓ Connect Visual Studio to Azure DevOps (TFVC) using Team Explorer.
✓ Check in your code to automatically trigger the build and create a Deployable Package.

──────────────────────────
🚀 About This D365 Development Series
──────────────────────────

This series goes beyond basic tutorials to show you how real-world Dynamics 365 (D365FO) projects are built from start to finish. We'll build a complete, end-to-end "Automated Customer Tiering System" for a fictional client, Bluestone Industrial Components (BIC).

You'll see every step of a production-ready solution, from setup to deployment, covering:
➤ Core X++ Development: Extending tables and forms (CustTable), creating Enums, and implementing custom business logic using Chain of Command (CoC).
➤ Automation: Building robust, automated batch jobs with the SysOperation Framework.
➤ APIs & Integration: Creating Data Entities to build secure OData REST APIs and for Data Management Framework (DMF) exports.
➤ Event-Driven Architecture: Firing real-time alerts from D365 to Azure Logic Apps using Business Events.
➤ Business Intelligence: Connecting D365 to Power BI to build an interactive sales dashboard.
➤ DevOps & ALM: Setting up a complete CI/CD pipeline in Azure DevOps, managing source control (TFVC), and automating builds.

────────────────
💻 Tools & Technologies
────────────────

🔹Dynamics 365 Finance & Operations (D365FO)
🔹X++
🔹Visual Studio 2019
🔹Lifecycle Services (LCS)
🔹Azure DevOps (ADO)
🔹SQL Server Management Studio (SSMS)
🔹Power BI Desktop
🔹Azure Logic Apps

───────────────────
💬 Feedback & Future Topics
───────────────────

This series covers the core components of a practical, end-to-end D365 project. I know there are many more topics we could dive into, from advanced debugging to complex form patterns.

I welcome your feedback and ideas! If there's a specific D365 topic you'd like to see covered in a future video, please share your suggestions in the comments section below.

videoTitle: The DevOps Godfather on AI's "Dark Factory" Problem
videoDescription:
Organizations are resisting the 'dark factory' model, not because of a lack of technological capability, but due to unprepared structures and mindsets. Coding agents are ready, but companies aren't set up for their seamless integration. Just like continuous delivery faced skepticism in 2009, autonomous coding agents now challenge existing frameworks and require a paradigm shift from developers as coders to orchestrators of systems. The shift isn't about better technology; it's about rethinking the roles and processes within an organization. Developers must evolve from technical craftsmanship to a conductor role in a system-driven environment, changing how teams and platforms function.

Patrick Debois, known widely as the 'godfather of DevOps', brings unique insights to this discussion. Having witnessed similar skepticism with the continuous delivery movement, Debois now observes the parallels between the challenges faced then and the resistance faced by the 'dark factory' approach today. At Tessl, where he observes first-hand the dynamics of adopting autonomous code agents, he highlights how this shift influences collaboration, team dynamics, and the role of platform teams.

What we cover:
• Why do organizations resist AI's 'dark factory' model?
• How do team dynamics change when developers become agent orchestrators?
• Which two metrics are crucial for measuring agentic productivity?
• What role do platform teams play in coding agent integration?
• How to hire for AI-native engineering roles
• Making a strong business case for adopting agent-driven engineering

videoTitle: Towards Vehicle DevOps – Michael Fait at Automotive Europe 2023
videoDescription:
The software-defined vehicle brings a new dimension of complexity to in-vehicle software development. Today we observe in the industry that software is written, integrated, and tested in long cycles. However, receiving feedback and experiencing the functionality of the software early and often is crucial to avoid issues. Vehicle DevOps is a way of creating a constant development flow with short feedback cycles. In this talk Michael Fait highlights current challenges for in-vehicle software development, introduces the concept of Vehicle Devops, and discusses its approaches to increase engineering effectiveness.

Michael Fait, Head of Autonomous Vehicle Tech, Thoughtworks

videoTitle: Novo Nordisk accelerates life-changing research using Azure DevOps and GitHub

Novo Nordisk scientists and engineers work at the frontiers of discovery to defeat serious chronic diseases. The researchers frequently collaborate with external teams. For every new Novo Nordisk partner, the IT team had to provide new environments and access. Novo Nordisk built a delivery platform to deploy its research collaboration platform in a multi-cloud setup on top of GitHub with integration from Azure DevOps. The fast, compliant delivery of the solution is a major benefit of teaming with Microsoft. The time to bring on new independent research teams has decreased from three to six months to only several hours. Novo Nordisk can now unlock synergies in a partnership or a consortium in methods development, biological analysis, and shared data science learning.

videoTitle: How We Fixed a 502 Bad Gateway in Production | Real DevOps Incident (Day 7)
videoDescription:
🚨 Day 7 of the DevOps in ARIA – Real-Time Scenario Series

Scenario:
Production just went down with a 502 Bad Gateway after a critical deployment. Jenkins pipeline triggered it, the deployment failed — and users were impacted.

🎯 Here’s how we handled it in real time:

Checked logs — the app was failing health checks

Root cause: a missing production environment variable

Rolled back the deployment safely using Helm

Fixed the configuration and stopped further rollouts

Patched the CI/CD pipeline to catch such issues early

🎥 Watch this short video to learn how real DevOps teams fix issues fast under pressure — and how you can too.

Takeaway:
Handling incidents is not just about tools — it’s about staying calm, investigating smartly, and improving your pipeline for the future.

videoTitle: Kubernetes at Mercedes-Benz | Philipp Bormann & Jens Erat | The DEVOPS Conference - Copenhagen, 2022
videoDescription:
How did Kubernetes change the game for software engineers at Mercedes-Benz?

Years ago, software engineers faced hard times at Mercedes-Benz: spreadsheet operations, manual processes, grown infrastructure, and strict governance. A grassroots initiative of engineers accepted the challenge to change the game – and their silver bullet was Kubernetes.

Join us on our journey from introducing Kubernetes 0.9 on managed servers to an on-premises self-service cloud platform with close to 1000 clusters on Cluster API. You will learn about our stake in transforming a data center with a young team that mostly did not know enterprise processes before.

We will take you back on our journey, including some technical details about the challenges we faced, our solutions to those, and lessons learned on the way.
---
Speakers:

Philipp Bormann, Platform Architect at Mercedes-Benz Group AG

After 10 years as a Network Engineer, Philipp became a Platform Architect for on-premises cloud platforms at Mercedes-Benz Group. He is one of the founding members of the company’s largest Kubernetes platform that helps to transform Mercedes-Benz into a digital car manufacturer.

videoDescription:
Manage & Secure Kubernetes Cluster Policies via OPA Gatekeeper. #opa #devops #gatekeepers 

Timestamps:

Theory/Concepts : 00:00
Hands on/Practical : 09:00

github repo : https://github.com/RohanRusta21/opa-gatekeeper.git

Concepts :

OPA Gatekeeper: Policy and Governance for Kubernetes

What is OPA:

The Open Policy Agent (OPA) is an open-source, general-purpose policy engine that unifies policy enforcement across the stack. OPA provides a high-level declarative language that lets us specify policies as code and simple APIs to offload policy decision-making from our software. We can use OPA to enforce policies in microservices, Kubernetes, CI/CD pipelines, API gateways, and more. 
In kubernetes, OPA uses admission controllers.

What is OPA Gatekeeper?

OPA Gatekeeper is a specialized project providing first-class integration between OPA and Kubernetes.
OPA Gatekeeper adds the following on top of plain OPA:
● An extensible, parameterized policy library.
● Native Kubernetes CRDs for instantiating the policy library (aka “constraints”).
● Native Kubernetes CRDs for extending the policy library (aka “constraint templates”).
● Audit functionality.

Why you need Gatekeeper?

As a Platform DevOps engineer managing multiple Kubernetes clusters for various projects, you face challenges when users deploy applications without adhering to best practices. Key issues include:
  1.     Lack of ownership unless users apply labels themselves.
  2.     No resource limits, leading to high costs.
  3.     Untrusted images impacting other applications.
  4.     Security and best practice violations across clusters.

To address these, we need governance to enforce limits and rules via policies. OPA Gatekeeper can be configured to implement these policies, ensuring best practices are followed.

videoTitle: Neurodiversity and the Essence of DevOps - Jeff Sussna
videoDescription:
It’s been gratifying to see the DevOps community take up the challenge of making empathy the essence of what we do. We should be proud of ourselves as an example to other organizational transformation approaches. We still, though, have room to grow. Whether it’s NoOps, or cloud-native chauvinism, or labeling people on the autism spectrum as lacking the capacity for empathy, we create subtle separations and exclusions through language and practice.

I would like to use my experience as a person with autism to reflect on the true meaning of empathy as the essence of DevOps. People on the spectrum are typically viewed as lacking something. In the process, our strengths and value get ignored. Real empathy means looking for wisdom and capability across differences. How do we do that in a comprehensive way? What are the obstacles to doing so in our current approaches to DevOps? How can overcoming those obstacles provide a model for digital transformation, and for healthy organizations, that transcends dev and ops?

Github Repo : https://github.com/RohanRusta21/demo_rabbitmq.git

Timestamp:
Understand Concept : 00:00
RabbitMQ Hands-on : 22:06

🧠 1. What Is RabbitMQ?

RabbitMQ is an open-source message broker — it acts as a middleman between different parts of a system that need to communicate asynchronously.
It uses the AMQP (Advanced Message Queuing Protocol) as its core protocol.

In simpler terms:

It receives messages from producers (applications sending data),

Stores them temporarily in queues,

And delivers them to consumers (applications receiving data).

This helps decouple systems — the sender and receiver don’t need to be active at the same time.

⚙️ 2. Why Use RabbitMQ?

✅ Decoupling – Producers don’t need to know who consumes messages.
✅ Asynchronous communication – Improves system responsiveness.
✅ Load balancing – Messages can be distributed across multiple consumers.
✅ Reliability – Ensures message delivery even if parts of the system fail.
✅ Scalability – You can add more queues or consumers easily.
✅ Flexible routing – Decide how messages flow using exchanges and routing keys.

🔩 3. Core RabbitMQ Concepts
🏭 Producers

Applications that send messages to RabbitMQ.
They don’t send messages directly to a queue but to an exchange.

🎯 Exchanges

An exchange routes messages to queues based on routing rules.

Exchange types:

Type Behavior Example Use Case
Direct Routes messages to queues whose binding key exactly matches routing key Task queues
Fanout Broadcasts all messages to all queues bound to it Notifications, pub/sub
Topic Routes messages based on pattern matching (* and #) Selective subscriptions
Headers Routes based on header attributes Advanced filtering

videoTitle: What is Secure DevOps?
videoDescription:
It’s surprisingly easy for hackers to impersonate authorized users of your corporate Git environment. Why? Because your developers can access it using their personal accounts, which are not tied to a corporate identity. That makes it difficult for IT to control access. And because contributors can sign the author field of a commit with anything they like, IT can’t track who is really authoring these commits.

Just as bad, contributors are committing code on unauthorized machines, often without even logging into the Git web service, evading all access controls.

This leaves your software components vulnerable to unauthorized access and tampering, which can lead to malicious code getting distributed to all of your clients.

With Secure DevOps by Beyond Identity, you can ensure that only your developers check in code to your repo. And that all commits came from an authorized user and device. All without impacting software velocity.

Beyond Identity is the only secure-by-design IAM platform foundationally built to ensure only trusted users and secure devices can ever gain and maintain access.

What’s the goal of Platform Engineering? Platform Engineering focusses on the building the infrastructure and the systems that are needed for running your applications and supporting your application throughout the software life cycle. So,  the goal  is to support the developers in the organisation and treat them as customers. That’s why we have in platform engineering the concept of IDP Internal developer platform.
 
So, this platform is treated as an actual product and the customers of the product are the developers.
What is the role of the IDP?
It is to create a thin layer on top of the toolchain that is used inside the organisation to standardise the processes and help developers to have one way to deploy into production

videoTitle: devopsdaysNYC 2020 - Day 2 - Thomas Limoncelli - Low-Context DevOps
videoDescription:
Low-Context DevOps: Helping DevOps find answers faster

Problem: Knowledge frustration is when siloed knowledge blocks you from doing your job. Yes, you can escalate or bother another coworker, but wouldn’t it be better if you had the instructions you needed when you needed it? Knowledge frustration is common for new people getting up to speed, experienced people moving between projects, and oncall engineers that receive an alert they’ve never seen before.

Solution: In this talk, I’ll show how to use the anthropology concept of high-context/low-context societies to eliminate knowledge frustration on DevOps/SRE teams. The result is improved productivity, continuous improvement, and a more enjoyable work environment.

Edward T. Hall was an American anthropologist who coined the phrase “high-context culture,” a culture where there are many unspoken rules. One must know a large amount of context to survive. Low-context cultures have the rules explicitly stated. This model describes engineering teams as well.

This is a talk about how to create a low-context culture where documentation is created incrementally, maintained continuously, and available just in time. Eliminate the “I’ll document it later” syndrome.

What is Liquibase, and why is database version control becoming an important skill for modern software development and DevOps careers?

In this Liquibase tutorial for beginners, we explain how Liquibase works as a database change management and deployment tool used by developers, DBAs, DevOps engineers, and software teams to manage database changes safely across Development, QA, UAT, and Production environments.

Liquibase works like Git for databases. Just as Git tracks application code changes, Liquibase tracks database schema changes using changelogs and changesets. Instead of manually running SQL scripts across multiple servers, teams can define database changes as code and automate database deployments through CI/CD pipelines.

You’ll understand the fundamentals of Liquibase, database version control, database migration, schema management, changelogs, changesets, CI/CD automation, DevOps, and database deployment.

videoTitle: Every DevOps Tool Explained (And the Only 10 You Need in 2026)
videoDescription:
There are over 1,000 tools in the CNCF landscape, and every single one claims to be essential for DevOps. Most of them are not. The ones that are fall into about 10 categories that have barely changed in a decade.

In this video I walk you through the entire DevOps toolchain: every category, the tools that actually matter inside each one, and what each one is genuinely good for. From Git and CI/CD to containers, Kubernetes, Terraform and OpenTofu, GitOps with Argo CD, observability, security, platform engineering, and the new AI layer (MCP, Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenClaw, Hermes Agent).

The biggest mistake I see junior engineers make is learning tools instead of learning the category the tool sits in. Tools get replaced. Categories don't.

⏱️ Chapters
0:00 1,000+ tools, 10 categories
0:38 The mental model
1:06 Prerequisites: Linux and networking
1:17 Version control (Git, GitHub, GitLab)
2:09 Continuous integration (GitHub Actions, Jenkins, GitLab CI)
3:09 Containers (Docker, containerd, Podman, registries)
4:01 Orchestration (Kubernetes, Helm, Kustomize, Lens)
5:15 Infrastructure as code (Terraform, OpenTofu, Pulumi, Spacelift)
7:04 Configuration management (Ansible, Chef, Puppet)
7:47 CD and GitOps (Argo CD, Flux, Argo Rollouts)
8:52 Observability (Prometheus, Grafana, OpenTelemetry)
9:50 Security (Trivy, Vault, OPA, Kyverno, Falco)
10:51 Platform engineering and the AI layer (Backstage, MCP, AI agents)
13:42 The stack I'd learn if I started today
14:12 The category is the skill

🧰 The stack I'd learn first
Git, GitHub Actions, Docker, Kubernetes, Terraform, Ansible, Argo CD, Prometheus and Grafana, Trivy and Vault, Backstage. One per category, learned deep. Swapping any of them out later takes a weekend, not a career.

📊 Sources
CNCF Annual Cloud Native Survey 2025: https://www.cncf.io/reports/the-cncf-annual-cloud-native-survey/
OpenTelemetry graduates CNCF (May 2026): https://www.cncf.io/announcements/2026/05/21/cloud-native-computing-foundation-announces-opentelemetrys-graduation-solidifying-status-as-the-de-facto-observability-standard/

videoTitle: Your /loop dies when you close the terminal
videoDescription:
/loop behaves differently depending on whether you give it an interval, a prompt, both or neither.

With an interval and a prompt, Claude converts the interval to a cron expression and runs your prompt on that fixed schedule. With a prompt only, Claude picks the gap itself, somewhere between one minute and one hour, and prints the delay and the reason at the end of each pass. With neither, it runs a built-in maintenance prompt: continue unfinished work, tend the pull request on your branch, then cleanup when nothing is pending.

All three land in the same scheduled task list, so you can list or cancel them the same way. Esc clears the pending wakeup while a loop is waiting.

The limit worth knowing: tasks only fire while Claude Code is running and idle. Closing the terminal or letting the session exit stops them. Backgrounding the session carries /loop tasks into a background session that keeps running without a terminal. Run /bg inside the session to do that, or press the left arrow on an empty prompt, which backgrounds it and opens agent view in one step. claude agents shows every background session on one screen.

/loop needs Claude Code 2.1.72 or newer.

💻  Commands Used to Configure the Permanent Tunnel

cloudflared tunnel login

cloudflared tunnel create jenkins-lab-jenkinsdevop-space

cloudflared tunnel route dns jenkins-lab-jenkinsdevop-space jenkinslab.jenkinsdevops.space


# Check config

-----
cat ~/.cloudflared/config.yml
tunnel: 77405485-1f7f-4430-916d-22b458bfee71
credentials-file: /home/rohit/.cloudflared/77405485-1f7f-4430-916d-22b458bfee71.json
ingress:

  - hostname: jenkinslab.jenkinsdevops.space
    service: http://localhost:8080

  - service: http_status:404

------

# Run tunnel

cloudflared tunnel run jenkins-lab-jenkinsdevop-space


# Install as service

sudo cloudflared --config /home/rohit/.cloudflared/config.yml service install

# Enable service

sudo systemctl enable cloudflared

# Start service

sudo systemctl start cloudflared

# Check service status

sudo systemctl status cloudflared

# View live logs

sudo journalctl -u cloudflared -f

videoTitle: Your app has 12 users and 9 microservices #Shorts
videoDescription:
Twelve users. Nine microservices. We need to talk.

In a monolith, fetching a user is one function call — nanoseconds, and it cannot time out. In microservices it's an HTTP call, a timeout, a retry, a circuit breaker and a prayer. Your database transaction is gone, replaced by eventual consistency: your data is correct, eventually, probably. And local setup is now fifteen containers and a laptop that sounds like a jet engine.

This isn't just a small-team problem. An Amazon Prime Video team merged a distributed monitoring system back into one process and cut its infrastructure cost by over 90% (AWS Prime Video Tech blog, March 2023 — one team, one component, not all of Prime Video). Segment did the same thing after passing 140 services and published a post called "Goodbye Microservices" (Segment engineering blog, July 2018).

Microservices solve an organisational problem wearing the costume of a technical one. Hundreds of engineers, clear domain boundaries, genuinely different scaling needs — yes. Six devs and one Jira board — build a modular monolith and extract a service when the pain is real.

Full breakdown on the channel: four costs, both case studies, and the honest case for when microservices are the right call.

Every diagram, terminal and dashboard here is drawn in code. Narration and sound effects generated with ElevenLabs.

videoTitle: Terraform Remote State and State Locking, Before Two Runs Collide
videoDescription:
🚀 The Automation Stack — Bite-sized tech for developers who want to stay ahead.

Terraform remote state and state locking let teams store state remotely in S3 and lock it, so two engineers cannot erase each other's work, and the classic DynamoDB lock is now deprecated in favor of S3's own lock file.

WHY ONE STATE FILE BREAKS ON A TEAM

By default the state file sits on one laptop. The docs spell out the problem. "When working with Terraform in a team, use of a local file makes Terraform usage complicated because each user must make sure they always have the latest state data before running Terraform and make sure that nobody else runs Terraform at the same time."

REMOTE STATE

So teams share the file. "With remote state, Terraform writes the state data to a remote data store, which can then be shared between all members of a team." On AWS that store is usually one object in an S3 bucket.

THE HOLE IN A SHARED FILE

Sharing alone does not protect it. Amazon's own S3 guide says "Amazon S3 does not support object locking for concurrent writers. If two PUT requests are simultaneously made to the same key, the request with the latest timestamp wins." So the later save replaces the earlier one, and what the first run built keeps running, untracked.

THE FIX IS A LOCK

"Terraform will lock your state for all operations that could write state." Anyone else is stopped with "Error acquiring the state lock" and the lock's details, including who holds it, and "If state locking fails, Terraform does not continue." On AWS the classic lock lived in a second service, a DynamoDB table with a partition key named LockID.

THE TWIST. THAT DYNAMODB LOCK IS DEPRECATED

THE BACKEND BLOCK

  terraform {
    backend "s3" {
      bucket       = "example-bucket"
      key          = "path/to/state"
      region       = "us-east-1"
      use_lockfile = true
    }
  }

The bucket, key and region are the docs' own example values. use_lockfile "Defaults to false", so the lock stays off until you set it. "When you change a backend's configuration, you must run terraform init again", and the option below "will attempt to copy existing state to the new backend".

  terraform init -migrate-state

HOW S3 HOLDS THE LOCK BY ITSELF

Terraform writes a small lock file next to the state, the key plus .tflock, with an If-None-Match header, so the write only succeeds if no file with that name exists yet. Amazon's conditional-writes guide says "If multiple conditional writes or copies occur for the same object name, the first write operation to finish succeeds. Amazon S3 then fails subsequent writes with a 412 Precondition Failed response." The second engineer is refused, and Terraform stops.

MOVING OFF DYNAMODB

You do not have to switch in one step. "To support migration from older versions of Terraform that only support DynamoDB-based locking, the S3 and DynamoDB arguments can be configured simultaneously." Terraform 1.10's changelog adds "When used with DynamoDB-based locking, locks will be acquired from both sources."

A LOCK LEFT BEHIND

If unlocking fails, the lock stays. The docs on clearing it are blunt. "Be very careful with this command. If you unlock the state when someone else is holding the lock it could cause multiple writers. Force unlock should only be used to unlock your own lock in the situation where automatic unlocking failed."

  terraform force-unlock LOCK_ID

PROTECT THE BUCKET

"It is highly recommended that you enable Bucket Versioning on the S3 bucket to allow for state recovery in the case of accidental deletions and human error."

Share the state. Lock the state. Only ever unlock your own lock.

videoTitle: Linux Commands for DevOps and SRE: grep, awk, sed, find and More
videoDescription:
10 Linux commands every DevOps engineer and SRE should know: grep, awk, sed, find, head, tail, sort, uniq, wc and cut. For each one, you get the 2 to 3 options you will actually use on the job, with real examples on nginx logs and system files.

Master these and you can answer questions about your system in seconds, not minutes.


COMMANDS FROM THIS SESSION

1. grep
Search for a string (add -i to ignore case):
grep "error" error.log
Search recursively through a directory:
grep -r "error" /var/log
Match 4xx and 5xx status codes with extended regex:
grep -E "4[0-9]{2}|5[0-9]{2}" access.log

2. awk
Print columns 1 and 6, with ":" as the separator:
awk -F: '{print $1 "   " $6}' /etc/passwd
Print lines where column 1 matches a value:
awk '$1 == "127.0.0.1"' access.log
Search for text and print specific columns:
awk '/error/ {print $17 $18}' error.log

3. sed
Replace every occurrence and print the result:
sed 's/10.0.2.200/10.0.2.120/g' /etc/nginx/conf.d/backend.conf
Replace inside the file itself:
sed -i 's/10.0.2.200/10.0.2.120/g' /etc/nginx/conf.d/backend.conf
Replace every IP address using extended regex:
sed -i -E 's/[0-9]{1,3}\.[0-9]{1,3}\.[0-9]{1,3}\.[0-9]{1,3}/127.0.0.1/g' /etc/nginx/conf.d/newbackend.conf

4. find
Find files by name:
find . -name "*.log"
Find files modified in the last 2 days:
find /var/log -type f -mtime -2
Run a command on every match:
find . -name "*.log" -exec gzip {} \;

5. head
First 10 lines:
head access.log
First 30 lines:
head -n 30 access.log

6. tail
Last 10 lines:
tail access.log
Last 30 lines:
tail -n 30 access.log
Follow the file live:
tail -f access.log

7. sort
Alphabetical sort:
ls | sort
Numeric sort, smallest directory first:
du -hk -d 1 | sort -n
Sort file systems by usage, highest first:
df -kh | sort -rk5

8. uniq
Unique client IPs sending bad requests:
grep " 400 " /var/log/nginx/access.log | awk '{print $1}' | sort | uniq
The same, with a count for each IP:
grep " 400 " /var/log/nginx/access.log | awk '{print $1}' | sort | uniq -c

9. wc
Count lines:
wc -l access.log
Count lines, words and characters:
wc access.log

10. cut
Extract fields 1 and 2:
cut -d: -f1,2 /etc/passwd
Extract fields 1 to 3:
cut -d: -f1-3 /etc/passwd

TWO ONE-LINERS FROM THIS SESSION

Top 10 client IPs hitting your server:
awk '{print $1}' /var/log/nginx/access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -n 10

Largest log files on your system:
sudo find /var/log -type f -name "*.log" -exec du -k {} \; | sort -rn | head -n 5

videoTitle: Latency vs Throughput vs Bandwidth Explained in 60 Seconds
videoDescription:
What’s the difference between latency, throughput, and bandwidth?

They sound similar, but in DevOps and cloud engineering, they describe very different performance characteristics.

Latency: How long does it take?
Throughput: How much work gets done per second?
Bandwidth: How much data can the connection carry?

And remember: more bandwidth does NOT automatically mean lower latency.

If you’re learning DevOps, Cloud Engineering, SRE, or networking, understanding this distinction will help you troubleshoot systems much faster.

videoTitle: OpenShift Dev Spaces Multi-Tenant Setup: The Gateway Quota Trap
videoDescription:
🚀 The Automation Stack — Bite-sized tech for developers who want to stay ahead.

The cluster rejected a developer's workspace. Not their code. A container nobody on the team ever wrote.

THE NEWS. Red Hat Developer published a blueprint for running OpenShift Dev Spaces as one shared, multi-tenant platform (October 9, 2026, by Ajay Kanse), tested on OpenShift 4.20.16 and Dev Spaces 3.26. Laptops drift, so every workspace runs as a container on the cluster, defined by a devfile kept in Git.

THE BLUEPRINT. Four namespaces: the operator in openshift-devspaces, its CheCluster config in devspaces-checluster (kept apart so the operator cannot overwrite custom settings), the extension server locked down in devspaces-openvsx, and one sandbox per developer, named username-devspaces. Auto-provisioning is off; a self-service step creates each sandbox with cost labels, a ResourceQuota and a LimitRange.

TWIST 1, THE GATEWAY QUOTA TRAP. A quota that counts CPU limits makes every container in a pod declare one. Dev Spaces adds a container you never wrote to every workspace, che-gateway. When it has no CPU limit, the pod is refused, and the quota error names che-gateway as the container missing limits.cpu. A quota violation is a 403 Forbidden. We read the operator source, che-operator 7.123.0, with the same lines at 7.110.0. It deletes the gateway's CPU limit on purpose whenever the namespace has no LimitRange and the CheCluster sets none, because a throttled container fails in ways that are hard to trace (Eclipse Che issue 22198). And the Kubernetes quota code (v1.33.0) calls its own per-container rule a mistake, kept for backward compatibility.

THE FIX. Give the gateway its own limit in the CheCluster, spec.devEnvironments.gatewayContainer.resources.limits.cpu set to 500m, which is half a CPU. Or give the namespace a LimitRange, and the operator keeps the gateway's limit. On screen, a line-for-line Python port of the quota check reproduces the refusal and admits both fixes; it is a port of the Go source, not a run of a real API server.

TWIST 2, THE CEILING IS PER CONTAINER. Every container gets a default and a ceiling, up to 4 CPUs. The ceiling applies to each container, so a workspace with 3 containers can take 12 CPUs. The namespace quota is the real cap. Each workspace also gets its own block volume, so cleanup is one delete.

TWIST 3, A STOPPED WORKSPACE IS NOT FREE. It still sits in etcd, the cluster's database. The article puts about 6,000 stopped workspaces at roughly 2.5 GB, past etcd's default limit of 2 GiB; etcd's own docs suggest at most 8 GiB. So idle workspaces are stopped after 4 hours, and a monthly cleanup job deletes any workspace not started in 30 days.

THE RULE. Limit every container. Cap every namespace. Expire every workspace.

Every code card on screen is checked. The operator and Kubernetes lines are verbatim from the tagged source, and the CheCluster, DevWorkspaceOperatorConfig and devfile YAML validate against the operators' own schemas.

videoTitle: Kubernetes Liveness Probe Restart Loop: How One Missing Binary Did It
videoDescription:
🚀 The Automation Stack — Bite-sized tech for developers who want to stay ahead.

A healthy Kubernetes worker was killed over and over, and its code was fine. The cause was one command missing from its container image. Cloud Native Now published the case on 25 September 2026, and the fix is a clean lesson in what liveness and readiness probes each actually do.

THE SETUP. A background Node.js worker pulled jobs from Redis. It served no web traffic, so it had no HTTP route. Its liveness probe was an exec probe that ran pgrep to find the worker process by name.

TURN 1, THE CHECK NEVER RAN. The slim runtime image did not contain pgrep. The kubelet could not run the check, and in the kubelet's own source (pkg/kubelet/prober/prober.go) a probe that errors out is returned as a failure. With the default failureThreshold of 3, three misses in a row mean a restart, and each restart waits longer (10 s, 20 s, 40 s and so on, capped at 5 minutes by default). The container ended up in CrashLoopBackOff, while the worker had been consuming jobs normally the whole time.

TURN 2, THE WEAK QUESTION. Installing pgrep would make the command run, but a process match only proves a process exists. It says nothing about whether the worker can reach Redis, take a job or finish one.

THE FIX. A tiny HTTP server inside the worker, on a health port that only the pod can reach, with no Service in front of it. Liveness calls /health, which answers from the event loop with the worker count and uptime and never touches Redis, so one Redis outage cannot restart every replica at once. Readiness calls /ready, which pings Redis with a two-second timeout and answers 200 or 503.

    livenessProbe:
      httpGet: { path: /health, port: health }
    readinessProbe:
      httpGet: { path: /ready, port: health }

TURN 3, WHAT READINESS CANNOT DO. When readiness fails, Kubernetes keeps the container running and removes the pod from every matching Service. This worker has no Service. It pulls jobs straight from Redis, so a worker marked not ready keeps taking new jobs. The drain has to live in the app, which must pause or close its own consumer. On shutdown, the step that mattered was awaiting stopWorkers() before closing Redis.

THE CHECKLIST FROM THE ARTICLE. Run every exec probe inside the exact runtime image, not a development shell. Break Redis on purpose and confirm /ready returns 503 while /health stays 200 and the restart count does not move. Send SIGTERM with a job in flight and verify the queue actually drains.

videoTitle: Terraform Plan vs Apply Explained, the Yes That Destroyed a Server
videoDescription:
🚀 The Automation Stack — Bite-sized tech for developers who want to stay ahead.

terraform plan vs apply explained in two minutes. Learn the plan/apply workflow and why previewing changes prevents disasters, with every output taken from Terraform itself.

ONE LINE, ONE DESTROYED SERVER

Change one line of Terraform, the image a server boots from (an example), run apply and type yes. Terraform destroys that server and builds a new one. Nothing crashed. It did exactly what the code asked, and the plan said so right above the yes.

WHAT PLAN DOES

Plan reads what really exists, compares it with your code and proposes changes. "The plan command alone does not actually carry out the proposed changes" Read the symbols. A plus is create, a tilde is update in place, a minus is destroy, and minus slash plus is destroy and then create a replacement.

    # aws_instance.web must be replaced
  -/+ resource "aws_instance" "web" {
        ~ ami = "ami-0aaa1111" -＞ "ami-0bbb2222" # forces replacement
      }

In the AWS provider's own schema the image (ami) forces a replacement and the size (instance_type) does not, so changing only the size is an update in place. Same one line, very different result.

THE CATCH

Apply on its own makes a brand new plan, not the one you read. "When you run terraform apply without passing a saved plan file, Terraform automatically creates a new execution plan as if you had run terraform plan, prompts you to approve that plan, and performs the indicated operations." Skip the file and Terraform even prints a note. "You didn't use the -out option to save this plan, so Terraform can't guarantee to take exactly these actions if you run "terraform apply" now."

SAVE IT, READ IT, APPLY THE FILE

  terraform plan -out=tfplan
  terraform show tfplan
  terraform apply tfplan

"Terraform interprets the act of passing the plan file as the approval." So there is no second yes. And if another run changes things after you saved it, Terraform refuses with "Saved plan is stale" and says "The given plan file can no longer be applied because the state was changed by another operation after the plan was created."

A PREVIEW, NOT A PROMISE

"Terraform does not automatically roll back a partially-completed apply." What it created stays created. Fix the error, then plan again and apply again. "After you resolve the error, you must apply your configuration again"

GUARD WHAT YOU CANNOT LOSE

  resource "aws_db_instance" "orders" {
    # ...
    lifecycle {
      prevent_destroy = true
    }
  }

"Terraform rejects plans that would destroy the infrastructure object associated with the resource and returns an error." The refusal reads "Instance cannot be destroyed".

FAIL THE RUN ON ANY DELETE

The -auto-approve flag skips the question, and the docs warn that it covers deletes too. "Note that this includes destructive operations such as deleting resources." In automation, let a script read the saved plan as JSON instead.

  import json, subprocess, sys

  show = subprocess.run(["terraform", "show", "-json", "tfplan"],
                        capture_output=True, text=True, check=True)
  plan = json.loads(show.stdout)
  doomed = [rc["address"] for rc in plan.get("resource_changes", [])
            if "delete" in rc["change"]["actions"]]
  if doomed:
      sys.exit("plan deletes: " + ", ".join(doomed))
  print("no deletes, safe to apply")

Run against a saved plan that replaces the server, it exits non-zero and stops the job before apply ever starts.

Read the plan. Save the plan. Apply the file, and nothing else.

videoTitle: Pod Deleted: Who Replaces it?
videoDescription:
How does Kubernetes replace a deleted Pod? See how a Deployment, its ReplicaSet, and Pods work together—and what changes during a rollout or rollback.

A ReplicaSet keeps the requested number of matching Pods running. A Deployment manages the ReplicaSets as application versions change. The Pods run the app.

videoDescription:
Talk completo (49 minuti) al Reggio Emilia Full Stack:

Se l'applicazione è in un container e qualcuno riesce a leggere file arbitrari, tocca solo i file del container, non quelli del sistema host.

videoTitle: DevOps Engineer Salary — What You'll Really Earn (Junior to Architect)
videoDescription:
Three real DevOps engineer salaries: seventy thousand pounds, a hundred and sixty-five thousand dollars, thirty-five thousand pounds.
Every DevOps engineer salary figure here is labelled with where it came from and who it counted, junior to architect.

Most salary videos quote one number and call it the truth. The numbers disagree because they come from three different populations — job adverts, self-reported surveys, and recruiter placements — and each answers a different question. So every figure below carries its label, and none of them are averaged together. No courses to sell you, no dream to sell you.

*IN THIS VIDEO*
• Junior pay is ordinary, and junior openings are under four percent of the market
• Mid-level doubles the junior figure — the biggest single jump on the ladder
• Senior is only five thousand more, because the title is cheap
• Architect and staff is where it becomes life-changing, for very few seats
• Which single figure you should actually plan around, and why it isn't the biggest

videoTitle: DevOps Interview Practice With an AI
videoDescription:
DevOps interview practice, out loud: an AI interviews me, then hands me the notes.
Free community: https://www.skool.com/darrell-does-devops-8796/about

This is the opening segment of my Saturday office hours, cut on its own. An AI interviews me about my own homelab project and at the end it hands me the notes an interviewer writes down and never shows you. Most interviews stay polite whether you're landing it or bombing, and the only tell is whether the next question builds on what you just said. So I ran the interview on myself, live, answering with my voice instead of my keyboard, and read the debrief on stream. It put my K3s box on one of four bands that anyone who's worked a help desk already knows. The interviewer prompt is free in the community's Classroom. Run it on your project tonight.

Not sure where your gaps are? Free five-minute scan: https://scan.darrelldoesdevops.com

channelDescription:
For ops and sysadmins breaking into DevOps. Free community below.

You look at DevOps job postings, count forty tools, and quietly decide it's a two or three year project. It isn't. It's five areas, and you already own pieces of them if you came from ops.

I came from Windows and PowerShell, not Linux, and broke in the slow, scattered way before anyone drew me the map. So I drew it.

The real skill now isn't memorizing tools, and it isn't handing the work to AI either. It's using AI to learn faster while you do the reps yourself, until you understand the work well enough to catch the AI when it's wrong. That's the person who gets hired.

No faceless automation, no AI voice, no fifty-tool tutorials you'll forget by Friday. Just the map, the reps, and how to point AI at the parts you're stuck on.

videoTitle: Is DevOps Hard? The 3 Walls Beginners Hit, From the Hiring Side

videoTitle: CPU खाली, फिर भी Pod Pending? Kubernetes Requests समझें
videoDescription:
Kubernetes Pod Pending और FailedScheduling: Insufficient cpu का एक practical कारण समझें। Scheduler resource requests और node allocatable capacity देखता है, सिर्फ current CPU usage नहीं।

Commands:
kubectl describe pod POD -n NAMESPACE
kubectl describe node NODE
अपने Pod, namespace और node के नाम रखें। Events, Allocatable और Allocated resources देखें।

Illustrative single-container example: allocatable 2000m, existing CPU requests 1500m, remaining 500m. New request 1000m does not fit. If measured workload needs justify 500m, that request satisfies this CPU fit constraint; memory, affinity, taints, volumes and other constraints still apply. 1000m = 1 CPU. Adjust declared workload configuration based on measured needs, or add eligible capacity. Do not blindly remove requests. Pending can have other causes.

Natural AI narration: ElevenLabs, Raqib - Clear Documentary Presenter, Eleven v4. Original script and animation by NextGen Grind. Commands and output are illustrative.

videoTitle: The SRE's Job After AI Agents: What Changes
videoDescription:
This video is part of a series: How AI Agents are changing IT jobs: https://youtube.com/playlist?list=PLVqydu49tB3I

Will AI agents replace SREs and DevOps engineers? No, but they now take over the first response to an incident: sorting the alerts, investigating the outage and rolling back a bad release. Yet engineers still spend about a third of their time on repetitive manual work, and on real Kubernetes incidents the best AI model finds the root cause less than half the time. This is where the SRE job is going, and the on-call side of DevOps with it.

What you'll learn:

- What an operations week really looks like: alerts, on-call, releases, change approvals, capacity and cost, runbooks, postmortems and reliability work
- Which tasks AI agents take over: alert grouping, incident investigation, runbook fixes like restarts and rollbacks, status updates and postmortem drafts
- Why an agent's diagnosis can look right while the real cause is still there (ITBench-AA: the best model scored under 50%)
- Why AI adoption goes with faster delivery but less stable releases (Google's DORA research)
- What happened when an AI coding agent was allowed to fix an issue on its own at Amazon, and why Amazon added mandatory peer review for production access
- What stays human: setting the reliability target, leading the incident, approving what can't be undone and learning from failure
- The new skill, containing the blast radius: scope, stop conditions and recovery
- What this means if you are starting out, if you are an SRE or platform engineer, and if you manage releases

videoTitle: Declarative vs Imperative Infrastructure, Shuffle Your Deploy Code
videoDescription:
🚀 The Automation Stack — Bite-sized tech for developers who want to stay ahead.

Declarative vs imperative infrastructure explained in two minutes. Describing the desired end state vs scripting each step, and why Terraform and Kubernetes chose declarative.

SHUFFLE THE SCRIPT, SHUFFLE THE FILE

Here is a deploy script with its server step moved to the top.

  aws ec2 run-instances \
    --image-id ami-0abcdef1234567890 \
    --instance-type t3.micro --subnet-id $SUBNET
  VPC=$(aws ec2 create-vpc \
    --cidr-block 10.0.0.0/16 \
    --query Vpc.VpcId --output text)
  SUBNET=$(aws ec2 create-subnet \
    --vpc-id $VPC --cidr-block 10.0.1.0/24 \
    --query Subnet.SubnetId --output text)

Run here with the AWS CLI and no credentials, it fails on its first command with "aws: error: argument --subnet-id: expected one argument", because the subnet it needs does not exist yet.

THE HOW AND THE WHAT

A script is imperative. You write the how, one step at a time, and the order is the program. A Terraform file is declarative. You write what should exist, and the tool works out the steps. In Terraform's own words, "The Terraform language is declarative, describing an intended goal rather than the steps to reach that goal."

WRITTEN FIRST, BUILT LAST

  resource "aws_instance" "web" {
    ami           = "ami-0abcdef1234567890"
    instance_type = "t3.micro"
    subnet_id     = aws_subnet.app.id
  }

  resource "aws_subnet" "app" {
    vpc_id     = aws_vpc.main.id
    cidr_block = "10.0.1.0/24"
  }

  resource "aws_vpc" "main" {
    cidr_block = "10.0.0.0/16"
  }

The server block is written first, and it is still built last. Terraform reads the references between resources and works out the order itself, and its documentation says "The ordering of blocks and the files they are organized into are generally not significant". Measured here with Terraform 1.16.5, three linked blocks written web, app, main were created main, app, web. A script is driving directions, a declarative file is the address, and directions only work from the corner they started on.

ONE CHANGE, TWO WORLDS

Make the server bigger. A script needs new steps, in the right order, because Amazon's own guide says "You must stop your instance before you can change its instance type."

  ID=i-1234567890abcdef0
  aws ec2 stop-instances --instance-ids $ID
  aws ec2 wait instance-stopped --instance-ids $ID
  aws ec2 modify-instance-attribute --instance-id $ID \
    --instance-type Value=t3.small
  aws ec2 start-instances --instance-ids $ID

In the Terraform file, you change one word.

    instance_type = "t3.small"

THE CATCH, THE STEPS MOVED

Declarative does not remove the steps. It moves them into the tool. The AWS provider's docs say "Updates to this field will trigger a stop/start of the EC2 instance.", and its source code stops the instance, modifies the attribute and starts it again. Someone still wrote the how. It just lives in the tool, so your file only says what you want.

WHY KUBERNETES CHOSE IT TOO

The Kubernetes documentation calls an object a "record of intent", and says "this is your cluster's desired state." A command changes the live cluster and leaves no record except what is live.

  kubectl scale deployment/web --replicas=3

The same three replicas in a file can be reviewed before anything changes.

  apiVersion: apps/v1
  kind: Deployment
  metadata:
    name: web
  spec:
    replicas: 3

And the surprise, the same documentation still recommends commands "to get started or to run a one-off task in a cluster", and warns "Mixing and matching techniques for the same object results in undefined behavior."

Write what you want. Let the tool work out the how.

videoTitle: Your API can call a language model at localhost
videoDescription:

videoTitle: What Is Configuration Drift? Your Code Says 3, Production Runs 5
videoDescription:
🚀 The Automation Stack — Bite-sized tech for developers who want to stay ahead.

What is configuration drift? It is the gap between your code and what is really running, and manual changes cause real infrastructure to drift from code. Here is how Terraform sees it, and where it does not, run for real.

THE CODE SAYS THREE

Three nginx containers stand in for three servers, built by Terraform with the kreuzwerker/docker provider. Every line here was run on this machine with Terraform 1.16.5.

  resource "docker_container" "web" {
    count       = 3
    name        = "web-${count.index}"
    image       = docker_image.nginx.image_id
    memory      = 256
    memory_swap = 512

    labels {
      label = "managed-by"
      value = "terraform"
    }
  }

A QUICK FIX BY HAND

During an incident someone starts two more servers by hand. Five are running, and Terraform still prints "No changes. Your infrastructure matches the configuration." with exit code 0.

  $ docker run -d --name web-3 nginx:alpine
  $ docker run -d --name web-4 nginx:alpine
  $ terraform plan -detailed-exitcode
  No changes. Your infrastructure matches the configuration.
  and found no differences, so no changes are needed.
  $ echo $?
  0

HashiCorp's own definition, "This deviation is known as configuration drift." Terraform only checks the servers it manages. The two made by hand were never handed to it.

THE SECOND KIND

One server keeps running out of memory, so someone doubles it by hand. That server Terraform does manage, so its next check catches it.

  $ docker update --memory 512m web-0
  $ terraform plan -detailed-exitcode
    # docker_container.web[0] will be updated in-place
        ~ memory = 512 -＞ 256
  Plan: 0 to add, 1 to change, 0 to destroy.
  $ echo $?
  2

That line is not a warning. It is the next action. The official tutorial says "Terraform would attempt to revert your manual changes." The next deploy put the memory back to 256 here, and the crash you fixed comes back.

DETECT AND CORRECT

Check for drift on a schedule. The documentation for -detailed-exitcode says "2 = Succeeded with non-empty diff (changes present)", so a scheduled job can alert on exit code 2. Then pick a direction. Put the server back, or write the change into the code and review it like any change.

  -  memory      = 256
  +  memory      = 512

THE SERVERS IT NEVER SAW

Even after the next deploy, the two hand-made servers were still running.

  $ terraform apply -auto-approve
  Apply complete! Resources: 0 added, 1 changed, 0 destroyed.
  $ docker ps --format "{{.Names}}"
  web-4
  web-3
  web-1
  web-2
  web-0

So tag everything the code builds, then list what is really running. Docker's docs say "The label filter matches containers based on the presence of a label", and anything without the tag did not come from the code.

  $ docker ps --filter "label=managed-by=terraform" --format "{{.Names}}"
  web-1
  web-2
  web-0

Fix it in the code. Otherwise the code will undo it, or never see it.

channelDescription:
Infrastructure fails in ways too absurd to be fiction. Infra Pain turns real DevOps, SRE and sysadmin disasters into 60-second lessons: YAML betrayals, Friday deploys, 3am pages, Kubernetes doing exactly what you told it to (unfortunately). 

Every Short is a tiny postmortem, minus the blame, plus the jokes. New pain (almost) daily. Subtitles in English and Portuguese.

No production systems were harmed in the making of this channel. Several careers, maybe.
